words.shortDefinition: OWASP's ranked list of the ten most critical web application security risk categories, updated every few years.
words.simpleDefinition: The OWASP Top 10 is a ranked awareness document published by the Open Worldwide Application Security Project. It lists the ten most dangerous patterns attackers currently exploit across web applications, drawing on data from hundreds of organizations and millions of tested applications. The 2021 edition — the current authoritative version — is led by Broken Access Control, followed by Cryptographic Failures and Injection.
words.longDefinition: The OWASP Top 10 is the most-cited document in application security. It combines two inputs: empirical data from hundreds of contributing organizations covering millions of tested applications, and a community survey where practitioners rate emerging risks. Each category is scored on likelihood (prevalence, detectability, exploitability) multiplied by impact (technical and business consequences). The ranking shifts between editions as defensive practices improve — SQL Injection led the list for over a decade before dropping to third place in 2021 as parameterized query libraries became standard. The 2021 edition introduced three new categories: Insecure Design (A04), Software and Data Integrity Failures (A08), and SSRF (A10). Critically, the Top 10 is a risk-awareness document, not a compliance checklist — passing all ten categories does not make an application secure, it means the application avoids the ten most common failure patterns. OWASP maintains companion resources: the ASVS for structured verification, the WSTG for testing methodology, and the API Security Top 10 for REST/GraphQL-specific risks.
words.connector: Think of the OWASP Top 10 like a 'most-wanted' list for web application crimes — it tells defenders where the worst offenders cluster, not every possible offense.
words.techContext: Our quarterly security review maps every open finding to an OWASP Top 10 category so we can measure whether our control investments are hitting the highest-risk areas.
words.exampleSentence: When the new engineer asked where to start with web security, the tech lead pointed them to the OWASP Top 10 to understand the landscape before diving into any individual vulnerability.

words.etymology: OWASP stands for Open Worldwide Application Security Project (originally 'Open Web Application Security Project', updated 2023). The organization was founded in 2001; the Top 10 list has been published since 2003.

words.shortDefinition: Consolidated OAuth 2 specification that mandates PKCE, removes implicit flow, and tightens redirect-URI validation.
words.simpleDefinition: OAuth 2.1 is not a new protocol — it is a cleaned-up consolidation of OAuth 2.0 and all the security best practices (BCP 212 / RFC 9700) that accumulated over a decade of real-world use. The implicit flow, which returned tokens directly in browser URL fragments and caused widespread token leakage, is gone. PKCE is now mandatory for all clients including confidential server-side apps. Redirect URI matching must be exact, not prefix-based.
words.longDefinition: OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) was published in 2012. Over the following decade, several flows it defined turned out to be insecure, and a library of additional RFCs and best-current-practice documents accumulated. OAuth 2.1 (draft RFC) consolidates the result: it incorporates RFC 6749, RFC 6750 (Bearer tokens), RFC 7636 (PKCE), RFC 8707 (Resource Indicators), and OAuth 2.0 Security BCP (RFC 9700) into a single coherent document. Key changes: the Implicit flow (response_type=token) is removed; the Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC) flow is removed; PKCE is required for all authorization code flows regardless of client type; refresh tokens issued to public clients must be sender-constrained or rotate with each use; redirect URI matching must be an exact string comparison, not a prefix or pattern match. The consolidation matters because older OAuth 2.0 deployments that still use implicit flow or loose redirect URI matching are vulnerable to authorization code interception and token theft.
words.connector: Think of OAuth 2.1 as a security-focused update removing the unsafe shortcuts from the original spec — like a revised driver's-ed manual that removes the chapter saying it's sometimes okay to skip checking your mirrors.
words.techContext: We upgraded our authorization server to OAuth 2.1 mode, which required adding PKCE to our mobile app flows and switching the SPA from implicit to authorization code with PKCE.
words.exampleSentence: The security audit flagged our SPA for using the implicit flow, so we migrated to the authorization code flow with PKCE as required by OAuth 2.1.
words.etymology: OAuth derives from 'Open Authorization'; the 2.1 designation reflects a consolidating minor revision rather than a protocol redesign.

words.shortDefinition: OpenID Connect; identity layer on top of OAuth 2 that provides a standardized ID token for user authentication.
words.simpleDefinition: OAuth 2 solves authorization — it lets an app act on a user's behalf. But it says nothing about who the user is. OpenID Connect (OIDC) fills that gap by adding an ID token: a signed JWT containing the user's identity claims (sub, email, name). The app can verify the ID token's signature and trust the identity without building its own authentication protocol.
words.longDefinition: OpenID Connect 1.0 was published in 2014 by the OpenID Foundation. It sits as an identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0, adding three things: a standardized ID token (a signed JWT), a UserInfo endpoint the app can query for additional claims, and a Discovery document (/.well-known/openid-configuration) that describes the provider's endpoints and supported algorithms. The ID token contains: iss (issuer), sub (subject — stable unique user ID), aud (audience — must match your client_id), exp (expiry), iat (issued-at), and optionally nonce (for replay protection). Critical validation rules: verify the signature using the provider's public key (obtained from the JWKS endpoint), verify iss matches the expected provider, verify aud contains your client_id, verify exp is in the future, verify nonce matches what you sent (for implicit/hybrid flows). OIDC underpins nearly every modern SSO system — Google Sign-In, Apple Sign-In, GitHub OAuth, Okta, Auth0, and Cognito all implement OIDC. The separation of concerns is key: OAuth 2 handles 'can this app access resource X?'; OIDC handles 'who is this user?'
words.connector: Think of OIDC as the identity card layer on top of OAuth's access-permit layer — OAuth says 'you may enter', OIDC says 'and here is who you are'.
words.techContext: We use OIDC with our identity provider so the app receives a verified ID token on login — no password storage, no custom auth code, just signature verification.
words.exampleSentence: By integrating OIDC, the platform could verify the user's identity from any compliant provider without ever storing passwords or implementing its own authentication logic.
words.etymology: OpenID Connect combines 'OpenID' (the older federated identity standard, 2005) with 'Connect' to signal its role as the connector between OAuth 2 authorization and user identity.

words.shortDefinition: Demonstrating Proof of Possession; an OAuth 2.0 mechanism that cryptographically binds an access token to the client's private key, blocking token replay attacks.
words.simpleDefinition: DPoP stops a stolen OAuth token from being used by anyone except the original client. The client generates a key pair, includes the public key in a signed proof-of-possession JWT on every request, and the server verifies both the access token and that the request was signed by the matching private key. An attacker who intercepts the token cannot use it without also having the client's private key.
words.longDefinition: DPoP (Demonstrating Proof-of-Possession at the Application Layer, RFC 9449) is an OAuth 2.0 security extension that addresses a fundamental weakness of bearer tokens: a bearer token can be replayed by anyone who obtains it. DPoP binds the token to a client-generated asymmetric key pair. Mechanism: (1) the client generates an ephemeral key pair (EC P-256 or RSA-2048 recommended); (2) at the authorization server, the client sends a DPoP proof JWT — a short-lived, signed JWT containing the public key (in the jwk header), the current timestamp (iat), a unique jti, the HTTP method (htm), and the request URL (htu); (3) the authorization server issues a DPoP-bound access token containing a cnf (confirmation) claim with the jkt (JWK thumbprint) of the client's public key; (4) on every resource server request, the client sends both the DPoP-bound token and a fresh DPoP proof JWT; (5) the resource server verifies the token's signature, checks the cnf.jkt matches the public key in the DPoP proof, and that the proof is fresh (iat within a tolerance window) and unique (jti not recently seen). An attacker who steals the access token cannot use it because they lack the client's private key to generate a valid DPoP proof. DPoP is the successor to mTLS-bound tokens (RFC 8705) for environments where client certificates are impractical. It is the recommended binding mechanism for mobile OAuth clients and public clients (browser-based apps) where client secrets cannot be kept confidential.
words.connector: Think of DPoP like a wax seal on a letter — the token is the letter's contents, and the DPoP proof is a fresh seal on the envelope. Even if someone steals the letter, they can not reseal it with the same personal wax stamp; the recipient verifies both the contents and the seal's authenticity.
words.techContext: We implemented DPoP for our mobile OAuth flow: the app generates an EC key pair on first launch, and every token request and API call includes a DPoP proof. Token theft from network interception became harmless — the stolen token is unusable without the device's private key.
words.exampleSentence: After a security review flagged that stolen bearer tokens could be replayed from any host, the team replaced standard OAuth 2.0 bearer tokens with DPoP-bound tokens, ensuring that leaked tokens are cryptographically tied to the client that obtained them.

codeExample.code:
# Generating a DPoP proof JWT (RFC 9449)
import json, time, uuid, base64
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives.asymmetric import ec
from cryptography.hazmat.primitives import hashes, serialization
import jwt  # PyJWT

# Key pair generated once per client session
private_key = ec.generate_private_key(ec.SECP256R1())
public_key = private_key.public_key()

def make_dpop_proof(http_method: str, request_url: str) -> str:
    """Create a DPoP proof JWT for a single request."""
    public_numbers = public_key.public_numbers()
    jwk = {
        "kty": "EC", "crv": "P-256",
        "x": base64.urlsafe_b64encode(public_numbers.x.to_bytes(32, 'big')).rstrip(b'=').decode(),
        "y": base64.urlsafe_b64encode(public_numbers.y.to_bytes(32, 'big')).rstrip(b'=').decode(),
    }
    payload = {
        "jti": str(uuid.uuid4()),   # unique per request — prevents replay
        "htm": http_method,          # HTTP method
        "htu": request_url,          # URL (no query/fragment)
        "iat": int(time.time()),      # must be fresh (within ~60s)
    }
    return jwt.encode(payload, private_key, algorithm="ES256",
                      headers={"typ": "dpop+jwt", "jwk": jwk})

words.etymology: DPoP is an acronym for Demonstrating Proof of Possession; 'proof of possession' is a long-standing cryptographic concept meaning the holder demonstrates they control the private half of a key pair; RFC 9449 was published by the IETF OAuth working group in 2023.

words.shortDefinition: Taking over an authenticated user's session by stealing or forging their session token without compromising their credentials.
words.simpleDefinition: Session hijacking lets an attacker act as a logged-in user without knowing their password. If the attacker can steal the session cookie — through XSS, network interception, or a compromised subdomain — they can make requests as that user for as long as the session is valid. The attack works because HTTP is stateless: the session token is the only proof of identity on each request.
words.longDefinition: Session hijacking is an attack that targets the session management layer rather than the authentication layer. Once a user authenticates, the server issues a session token (typically stored in a cookie) that acts as a temporary credential for subsequent requests. If an attacker obtains this token, they can impersonate the user for the life of the session without knowing their password. Attack vectors: cross-site scripting (XSS steals cookies via document.cookie — mitigated by HttpOnly flag); network interception (plain HTTP or mixed content allows passive sniffing — mitigated by HTTPS + Secure cookie flag); cookie theft via subdomain compromise (a vulnerable subdomain can set cookies on the parent domain); cross-site request forgery paired with a predictable session token; physical access to browser storage. A stolen session token is equivalent to a stolen password for the session's duration: the attacker can read account data, initiate transactions, change credentials (often including email and password), and establish persistence. Prevention: HttpOnly flag prevents JavaScript access; Secure flag ensures the cookie is only sent over HTTPS; SameSite=Strict or Lax reduces cross-site transmission; short session lifetimes with absolute and idle timeouts limit the theft window; token rotation (issuing a new token after authentication and after privilege escalation) limits the value of a stale token; binding sessions to IP or user-agent fingerprint adds friction (though both are spoofable). Session hijacking through cookie theft via XSS is distinct from CSRF: hijacking steals the session itself; CSRF exploits the browser's automatic cookie attachment to make cross-site requests without needing to steal the token.
words.connector: Think of session hijacking like a pickpocket stealing your hotel room key card — they don't need to check in (authenticate) themselves; they just use your key for the rest of the day until it expires at checkout.
words.techContext: After deploying HttpOnly and Secure flags on session cookies and rotating session IDs on privilege escalation, the penetration test confirmed that an XSS vulnerability on the marketing page could no longer be used to hijack admin sessions.
words.exampleSentence: The XSS vulnerability in the comment field allowed an attacker to inject a script that exfiltrated session cookies to an external endpoint, enabling session hijacking for any user who viewed the compromised page.

codeExample.code:
# Flask: session cookie hardening against hijacking
from flask import Flask
import os

app = Flask(__name__)

# Secure session cookie configuration
app.config.update(
    SECRET_KEY=os.environ["SESSION_SECRET"],  # strong random secret, not hardcoded
    SESSION_COOKIE_HTTPONLY=True,              # no JavaScript access (blocks XSS theft)
    SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE=True,               # HTTPS only (blocks network sniffing)
    SESSION_COOKIE_SAMESITE="Lax",            # cross-site submission protection
    SESSION_COOKIE_NAME="__Host-session",     # __Host- prefix: Secure + no Domain attribute
    PERMANENT_SESSION_LIFETIME=1800,          # 30-minute absolute timeout
)

# Rotate session ID on login to prevent session fixation (a precursor to hijacking)
from flask import session
from flask_login import login_user

def login(user):
    session.clear()           # discard pre-login session
    login_user(user)          # establishes new authenticated session
    session.modified = True   # forces new session ID issuance

words.etymology: Session (from Latin sessio, 'a sitting'; a period of authenticated activity) + hijacking (originally aircraft seizure; adopted in computing for unauthorized takeover of a communication channel); the term entered security vocabulary with TCP session hijacking attacks in the 1990s.

words.shortDefinition: Fast Identity Online 2; the open standard combining WebAuthn and CTAP2 that enables phishing-resistant authentication using public-key cryptography instead of passwords.
words.simpleDefinition: FIDO2 is the technical standard that makes phishing-resistant authentication possible. It combines two sub-specifications: WebAuthn (the browser API) and CTAP2 (how external authenticators like YubiKeys talk to the browser). Together they allow a device or hardware key to sign a server challenge with a private key that never leaves the authenticator. The server verifies the signature against the stored public key — no password is transmitted or stored.
words.longDefinition: FIDO2 is an open authentication standard maintained by the FIDO Alliance and the W3C, comprising two specifications: WebAuthn (Web Authentication API, a W3C Recommendation) and CTAP2 (Client to Authenticator Protocol 2, a FIDO Alliance specification). WebAuthn defines the browser JavaScript API that relying parties (websites and apps) use to register and authenticate credentials. CTAP2 defines the protocol between a browser or operating system and an external authenticator (a hardware security key like a YubiKey, or a smartphone acting as a roaming authenticator). The underlying cryptographic mechanism: during registration, the authenticator generates a new asymmetric key pair for the relying party's rpId (the effective domain). The private key never leaves the authenticator's secure element. The server stores the public key alongside a credential ID. During authentication, the server sends a random challenge; the authenticator signs the challenge (plus client data including the origin) using the private key; the server verifies the signature. The origin binding is the key phishing-resistance property: the signed clientDataJSON includes the origin string, and the server's rpId must match — an assertion signed against phishing.example.com will fail validation on example.com. FIDO2 supports multiple authenticator types: platform authenticators (built into the device — Face ID, Windows Hello, Android biometric) and roaming authenticators (hardware security keys via USB/NFC/BLE). Passkeys are FIDO2 discoverable credentials that can sync across devices via platform keystores. NIST SP 800-63B classifies FIDO2 authenticators as AAL2 (platform) or AAL3 (hardware security keys with physical presence requirement).
words.connector: Think of FIDO2 like a bank vault system where the teller never asks for the combination — instead, they slide a challenge note through the slot, and the vault signs it using an internal mechanism the customer can't see or extract; the teller then verifies the signature, not the combination.
words.techContext: We registered YubiKeys as FIDO2 hardware authenticators for all privileged accounts; the WebAuthn ceremony's origin binding means that even a successful spear phishing attack leading to a lookalike login page cannot harvest usable credentials.
words.exampleSentence: The post-incident analysis showed that all compromised accounts had used SMS-based MFA; the four accounts protected by FIDO2 hardware keys were the only ones that survived the targeted phishing campaign uncompromised.
words.etymology: FIDO stands for Fast Identity Online, chosen by the FIDO Alliance (founded 2012) to emphasize speed and openness; '2' designates the second generation of the standard, which added WebAuthn as a browser API and extended the protocol to web use cases beyond the original U2F hardware-key standard.

words.shortDefinition: HTTP response header (successor to Feature-Policy) that controls which browser APIs and capabilities a page and its embedded iframes may access.
words.simpleDefinition: Permissions Policy is an HTTP header that lets a server declare which powerful browser features — camera, microphone, geolocation, payment, USB access, and many more — are allowed for the current page and for third-party content embedded in iframes. A page that doesn't need the camera should disable it; that way, a successful XSS attack still cannot activate it.
words.longDefinition: Permissions Policy (formerly Feature-Policy, renamed in 2020) is a W3C specification that gives server-side control over which platform APIs are available to a document and any embedded browsing contexts. It was motivated by the growing number of powerful browser APIs (Geolocation, Camera, Microphone, Web Bluetooth, WebUSB, screen capture, ambient light sensors, etc.) that JavaScript can access. A page that embeds third-party advertising scripts or user-generated iframes should restrict those scripts from accessing hardware APIs the page does not need. The header syntax is a structured-fields list: each directive is a feature name followed by an allowlist. The allowlist values are: * (any origin, including cross-origin iframes); 'self' (same origin only, not embedded iframes by default); a quoted origin string; 'none' (disabled entirely, including the top-level document). Example: Permissions-Policy: geolocation=('self'), camera=(), microphone=() disables camera and microphone entirely and restricts geolocation to the first-party origin. Granular iframe control: the allow attribute on an <iframe> element overrides the parent policy for that specific frame, allowing a video-conferencing embed to use camera and microphone while the rest of the page cannot. Key security use case: restricting cross-origin iframes from accessing payment APIs, sensors, or device identifiers. Not a substitute for CSP but a complementary header; together they form the modern security headers baseline. The Permissions-Policy header is supported in all major browsers as of 2022.
words.connector: Think of Permissions Policy like a hotel's master keycard system — the hotel (the server) decides in advance which rooms (browser APIs) each guest category (origin) can open; a third-party contractor embedded in the building (iframe) only gets keys to the specific rooms the hotel explicitly authorizes.
words.techContext: We added Permissions-Policy: camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=(), payment=() to all API responses; when a third-party analytics script was later found to attempt geolocation access, the browser silently blocked it without any application code change needed.
words.exampleSentence: After the compliance review required restricting third-party script access to device sensors, the team added a Permissions Policy header that disabled geolocation and camera for all cross-origin iframes with a single header line.

codeExample.code:
# Flask: send a restrictive Permissions-Policy header on all responses
from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)

# Define which features are permitted and for which origins
# Empty allowlist () = disabled for everyone, including the top-level document
PERMISSIONS_POLICY = (
    "camera=(), "
    "microphone=(), "
    "geolocation=(), "
    "payment=(), "
    "usb=(), "
    "web-share=(), "
    "display-capture=(), "
    "accelerometer=(), "
    "gyroscope=(), "
    "magnetometer=()"
)

@app.after_request
def add_security_headers(response):
    response.headers["Permissions-Policy"] = PERMISSIONS_POLICY
    return response

words.etymology: Permissions (from Latin permittere, 'to allow through') + Policy (Greek politeia, 'governance'); the header was originally called Feature-Policy when drafted in 2016, then renamed Permissions Policy in the W3C specification revision of 2020 to better reflect that it controls permissions granted to features rather than toggling features on and off.

words.shortDefinition: Cookie attribute controlling whether the browser sends a cookie on cross-site requests, mitigating CSRF.
words.simpleDefinition: The SameSite attribute tells the browser when to include a cookie on cross-site requests. Strict means never on cross-site navigation. Lax (the Chrome default since 2020) means only on top-level GET navigations — no cross-site POST, iframe, or fetch. None means send always (pre-2020 behavior), but requires Secure. Lax blocks the most dangerous CSRF vectors, but Strict provides the strongest protection at the cost of some UX friction.
words.longDefinition: SameSite was introduced as a draft RFC by Google engineers in 2016 and added to the HTTP Cookie specification (RFC 6265bis). It exploits the distinction between same-site and cross-site requests: a request is same-site if the top-level document origin and the resource origin share the same registrable domain (eTLD+1); otherwise it is cross-site. Three values: SameSite=Strict — cookie never sent on cross-site requests, including top-level navigations from other sites (breaks SSO-style 'continue where you left off' flows); SameSite=Lax — cookie sent only on same-site requests and on cross-site top-level navigations with safe HTTP methods (GET, HEAD); SameSite=None — cookie sent in all contexts, backward-compatible, requires the Secure flag. Chrome changed the default from None to Lax in 2020 (SameSite-by-default), which broke many CSRF-vulnerable apps by accident. Limitations: SameSite does not replace CSRF tokens entirely — a subdomain takeover or a same-site but cross-origin attack path can still bypass it; Lax allows cross-site GET, so state-changing GET endpoints remain vulnerable. The defense-in-depth approach: use SameSite=Lax (or Strict where UX allows) plus a CSRF token for sensitive state-changing operations.
words.connector: Think of SameSite like a party guest rule: Strict says your browser only brings cookies to parties hosted by the same family (site), while Lax says it can bring cookies when walking in the door but not while quietly slipping in through a side window.
words.techContext: After Chrome's SameSite-by-default rollout our legacy API's cross-site POST integrations stopped receiving session cookies, forcing us to audit every cross-site flow.
words.exampleSentence: Setting SameSite=Strict on our session cookie eliminated most CSRF vectors, but we kept CSRF tokens for the payment endpoints as an additional layer since SameSite alone cannot block same-site subdomain attacks.

words.shortDefinition: Attack exploiting server-side use of the HTTP Host header for routing or URL generation, causing cache poisoning, password-reset link hijacking, or SSRF.
words.simpleDefinition: The Host header tells a server which virtual host the request is for. If application code uses the Host header value to generate URLs — like password reset links — an attacker who controls the Host header can redirect those links to their own server. The most serious variant: if the application trusts an X-Forwarded-Host or X-Host override header, the attack requires no special network position.
words.longDefinition: Host header injection is a server-side vulnerability caused by trusting user-controllable input in the HTTP Host (or X-Forwarded-Host, X-Host, X-Forwarded-Server) headers without validation. The HTTP Host header is required in HTTP/1.1 and is normally set by the browser to match the URL the user navigated to — but in HTTP requests, the client controls the Host field. Attack scenarios: (1) Password reset poisoning — the application generates a password-reset link using the Host header value (e.g., https://{request.host}/reset?token=...). An attacker who can make the server use a malicious Host value (directly, or by injecting X-Forwarded-Host) gets the reset URL sent to the victim's email pointing to the attacker's server; when the victim clicks the link, the token is delivered to the attacker. (2) Web cache poisoning — a cache keyed only on the request URL (not the Host) may store and serve responses containing malicious links generated from an attacker-controlled Host header. (3) SSRF via Host header in internal routing — some frameworks and reverse proxies forward requests based on the Host header; a manipulated Host can redirect internal routing to unintended destinations. (4) Password reset via X-Forwarded-Host — many frameworks read X-Forwarded-Host from reverse proxy headers without filtering; if an end-user request can set this header it bypasses the primary Host protection. Prevention: never use the Host header to construct URLs in application code; use a configured application base URL instead; validate the Host header against an allowlist of known virtual host names; configure the web server or framework to reject requests with unexpected Host values.
words.connector: Think of host header injection like a forged return-address on an official letter — if the bank uses the return address from your incoming letter to send your password reset, an attacker who forges the return address receives the reset token even though you filed the original request.
words.techContext: We hardened the password-reset flow by using an explicit BASE_URL environment variable for link generation instead of request.host, and added a Host header allowlist in Nginx that rejects requests with unexpected Host values before they reach the application.
words.exampleSentence: The penetration tester demonstrated host header injection against the password-reset endpoint: by supplying X-Forwarded-Host: attacker.example.com, they caused password-reset emails to contain links pointing to their server, delivering tokens for arbitrary accounts.

codeExample.code:
# VULNERABLE: using request.host for URL generation
# def make_reset_link(token: str) -> str:
#     return f"https://{request.host}/reset/{token}"   # attacker controls Host

# SAFE: use a configured base URL, never user-supplied headers
import os
from flask import request, abort

APP_BASE_URL = os.environ["APP_BASE_URL"]  # e.g., "https://app.example.com"
ALLOWED_HOSTS = frozenset(os.environ.get("ALLOWED_HOSTS", "").split(","))

def validate_host():
    """Reject requests with unexpected Host headers."""
    host = request.host.split(":")[0]  # strip port
    if host not in ALLOWED_HOSTS:
        abort(400, "Invalid Host header")

def make_reset_link(token: str) -> str:
    """Use configured base URL, never request.host."""
    return f"{APP_BASE_URL}/reset/{token}"

words.etymology: Host (from HTTP/1.1 RFC 2616, the mandatory header identifying the target virtual host) + header (the metadata section of an HTTP message preceding the body) + injection (from SQL injection's framing of inserting attacker-controlled content into a trusted channel); documented and popularized in web security research circa 2010-2012.

words.shortDefinition: Hardening a TLS client to trust only specific certificates or public keys instead of any certificate signed by a trusted CA, blocking interception by rogue CA issuance.
words.simpleDefinition: Normally, a TLS client trusts any certificate signed by any CA in the device's trust store — including enterprise MITM proxies and any CA that issues a certificate for a domain it doesn't control. Certificate pinning makes the client additionally require that the certificate (or its public key) match a specific known value. A rogue or compromised CA can't mount an interception attack because the pinned value won't match.
words.longDefinition: Certificate pinning (also called public key pinning or SSL pinning) is a defense against attacks that use a trusted-but-malicious CA to issue a fraudulent certificate for a target domain. The standard TLS certificate validation verifies that the certificate is signed by a CA in the trust store and that the hostname matches — but it does not verify which specific certificate or key is in use. Any trusted CA (there are hundreds in the device trust store) can issue a certificate for any domain, enabling man-in-the-middle attacks by enterprise inspection proxies, compromised CAs, or nation-state actors. Pinning adds a second check: the client compares the server's certificate or public key against a pre-configured pin (a hash of the certificate's SubjectPublicKeyInfo bytes, or the raw DER-encoded certificate). The two pin types: certificate pinning (pins the exact certificate; fails on renewal unless pins are updated) and public key pinning (pins the public key, surviving certificate rotation while the key pair stays the same — recommended). Deployment: pin the leaf certificate's public key, but always include backup pins from the CA or an intermediate so that key rotation can be deployed before disabling the old key. HTTP Public Key Pinning (HPKP), the browser-based header form, was deprecated in 2018 after several high-profile sites accidentally pinned incorrectly and locked users out. Certificate pinning remains in active use in mobile applications, IoT device firmware, and internal services communicating with known endpoints. Risks: a pinning failure due to a botched rotation can cause a complete service outage; pins must be updated before the pinned certificate or key expires. For consumer mobile apps, consider whether the incremental security benefit outweighs the operational risk of a pin-rotation outage.
words.connector: Think of certificate pinning like a photo ID check at a secret meeting — TLS normally accepts any government-issued ID, but pinning says 'we only accept Alice's specific ID card, not just any valid government document'; a forged ID from a different government agency won't be accepted.
words.techContext: Our mobile banking app pins the public key of our API server's TLS certificate; the app ships with both the current key hash and a backup hash for the next rotation, giving us a safe key-change window.
words.exampleSentence: The penetration tester confirmed that even with a corporate MITM proxy installed and trusted on the test device, the mobile app's certificate pinning caused all API calls to fail the TLS handshake, preventing traffic inspection.
words.etymology: Certificate (from Latin certificare, 'to assure'; the TLS certificate that identifies the server) + pinning (fixing something in place, from Old English pinn, 'peg'); the metaphor is fixing the expected certificate value so that the client's trust cannot be redirected.

words.shortDefinition: Adaptive password hashing function with a tunable work factor; widely supported, but has a 72-byte input limit.
words.simpleDefinition: bcrypt is a password hashing function designed in 1999 that includes a cost parameter — higher cost means more iterations and a slower hash. The work factor can be increased over time as hardware improves without invalidating existing hashes. Its main limitation: inputs longer than 72 bytes are silently truncated, so very long passphrases have less entropy than they appear to.
words.longDefinition: bcrypt was designed by Niels Provos and David Mazières, published at USENIX 1999. It is based on the Blowfish cipher's key schedule, using an Expensive Key Setup (EKS) algorithm that makes each hash computation require a configurable number of rounds (2^cost). The cost parameter (typically 10-14) is embedded in the hash output, so the work factor can be increased for new hashes while old hashes remain verifiable. The output format ($2b$12$...) encodes version, cost, salt (22 chars), and hash (31 chars). The 72-byte truncation limit is the most consequential footgun: a password of 200 characters and one of 72 characters with the same first 72 bytes produce identical hashes. This makes passphrase-based approaches less secure than they appear. OWASP's current guidance recommends Argon2id as the first choice for new systems, with bcrypt as an acceptable alternative for existing systems. Minimum recommended cost factor: 10 (verified takes ~100ms on modern hardware), tuned annually. Unlike Argon2, bcrypt has no memory cost — it is purely CPU-bound, which means well-resourced GPU attacks are more efficient against bcrypt than against Argon2id.
words.connector: Think of bcrypt like an adjustable safe dial — you can increase the number of turns required as safecrackers get faster, keeping the opening time constant at about one second regardless of hardware generation.
words.techContext: Our legacy auth service still uses bcrypt at cost 12; we verify that hashing new passwords takes approximately 100ms on our application servers and increase the cost factor annually.
words.exampleSentence: The code review flagged that the registration endpoint accepted passwords up to 500 characters, but bcrypt silently truncates at 72 bytes, making the extra length illusory.
words.etymology: bcrypt combines 'b' from Blowfish (the cipher it is based on) with 'crypt', the Unix password hashing convention; designed by Niels Provos and David Mazières, published at USENIX 1999.

words.shortDefinition: OAuth 2.0 mechanism (RFC 7662) by which a resource server queries the authorization server to verify a token's validity and claims without possessing the signing key.
words.simpleDefinition: Token introspection lets a resource server ask the authorization server 'is this token still valid, and what does it represent?' — without the resource server needing to hold the signing key or decode a JWT itself. The authorization server responds with the token's active status, scopes, expiry, and subject. This is especially useful for opaque tokens (random strings without embedded claims) and for checking real-time revocation.
words.longDefinition: Token introspection is defined in RFC 7662 (OAuth 2.0 Token Introspection, 2015). It provides a protected endpoint at the authorization server that resource servers can call to validate a presented token. The resource server sends a POST request with the token value; the authorization server responds with a JSON object containing: active (boolean — whether the token is currently valid), scope (space-separated list of authorized scopes), client_id, username, token_type, exp (expiry), iat (issued at), nbf (not before), sub (subject), aud (audience), iss (issuer), and jti (token ID). Token introspection is valuable in several scenarios: opaque token validation (the token is a random identifier stored in the authorization server's database — the resource server cannot decode it without calling introspection); real-time revocation checking (a JWTs expiry cannot be shortened after issuance, but an introspection call can detect that the token was revoked before its expiry via logout or security event); microservices without shared keys (a resource server that does not hold the JWT signing key can validate tokens through introspection instead of JWK endpoint polling). Performance consideration: introspection adds a network round-trip per request; for high-throughput services, a short-lived local cache keyed on jti (with TTL shorter than min token lifetime) avoids per-request calls while preserving near-real-time revocation detection.
words.connector: Think of token introspection like a cashier calling the bank to verify a check rather than accepting it at face value — slower than a quick glance, but detects fraudulent or cancelled checks that a visual inspection would miss.
words.techContext: Our internal API gateway uses token introspection for all service-to-service calls; it caches introspection results for 30 seconds keyed on jti, giving us a manageable round-trip overhead while keeping the revocation window below a minute.
words.exampleSentence: After introducing token introspection, a user who revoked their session from a compromised device was denied access within 30 seconds — previously, their JWT would have remained valid until its 4-hour expiry.

codeExample.code:
# RFC 7662: token introspection at a resource server
import requests
from functools import lru_cache
from time import time

INTROSPECTION_ENDPOINT = "https://auth.example.com/oauth/introspect"
RS_CLIENT_ID     = "resource-server-client"
RS_CLIENT_SECRET = "rs-secret"  # stored in env, not hardcoded

@lru_cache(maxsize=4096)  # simple TTL-less cache; replace with TTL cache in production
def introspect(token: str) -> dict:
    """Query authorization server about a token's validity."""
    resp = requests.post(
        INTROSPECTION_ENDPOINT,
        data={"token": token, "token_type_hint": "access_token"},
        auth=(RS_CLIENT_ID, RS_CLIENT_SECRET),
        timeout=2,
    )
    resp.raise_for_status()
    return resp.json()

def require_valid_token(token: str, required_scope: str) -> dict:
    info = introspect(token)
    if not info.get("active"):
        raise PermissionError("Token inactive or revoked")
    if required_scope not in (info.get("scope") or "").split():
        raise PermissionError(f"Missing required scope: {required_scope}")
    return info

words.etymology: Token (from Latin tessera, 'a piece'; in computing, a credential representing an authenticated identity) + introspection (Latin introspicere, 'to look within'; examining the token's properties by querying the issuing authority rather than decoding the token itself).

words.shortDefinition: Targeted phishing attack using personalized details gathered from OSINT to deceive a specific individual or organization.
words.simpleDefinition: Regular phishing sends the same lure to millions of addresses. Spear phishing is targeted: the attacker researches the victim's name, role, colleagues, current projects, and company news, then crafts a message that looks credible to that specific person. A message from 'your CTO' referencing a real project with your real team members' names is far more convincing than a generic 'verify your password' email.
words.longDefinition: Spear phishing is a targeted social engineering attack in which the adversary researches a specific individual or group before crafting the lure. Unlike generic phishing (mass-volume, low personalization), spear phishing involves OSINT research: LinkedIn profiles for job titles and reporting relationships, GitHub profiles for projects and colleagues, company news for recent events (acquisitions, product launches), Twitter/X for personal interests and travel patterns. The attacker uses this research to construct messages that pass the credibility test a trained user would apply: correct names and titles of sender and recipient, references to real ongoing work, plausible requests (review this PR, approve this invoice, update your MFA device). Common delivery vectors: email with a malicious link or attachment; SMS/WhatsApp (smishing) from a spoofed number; LinkedIn message impersonating a recruiter or vendor. The attacks that breach large enterprises most often use spear phishing as initial access, including most supply chain compromises. LLMs have lowered the cost of spear phishing dramatically: an attacker can synthesize OSINT from multiple sources into grammatically perfect, culturally appropriate, personalized messages at scale. Key defenses: security awareness training emphasizing that impersonation is not detectable from style alone; out-of-band verification for sensitive requests; FIDO2 phishing-resistant MFA (so even a successful credential harvest does not yield login); email authentication (DMARC, SPF, DKIM) to block domain spoofing.
words.connector: Think of spear phishing as the difference between fishing with a net (cast wide, catch whatever comes) and hunting with a rifle (one carefully aimed shot at a specific target after studying their patterns) — the latter requires more preparation but has a higher success rate per attempt.
words.techContext: After a spear phishing campaign targeted three of our senior engineers using LinkedIn-gathered data and impersonated our CTO's email address, we deployed DMARC enforcement on all sending domains and migrated admin accounts to FIDO2 hardware keys.
words.exampleSentence: The attacker's spear phishing email referenced the victim's recent Slack messages and used their direct manager's name, making it indistinguishable from legitimate internal communication until the suspicious link was analyzed.

codeExample.code:
Spear phishing defense checklist

1. Email authentication (blocks domain spoofing — a prerequisite)
   - SPF: list authorized sending IPs in DNS TXT record
   - DKIM: sign outgoing mail with private key; recipients verify signature
   - DMARC: policy (reject/quarantine) + alignment enforcement + reporting
     Strict DMARC: p=reject; prevents From: spoofing of your domain

2. Phishing-resistant MFA (credential harvest becomes useless)
   - FIDO2 hardware keys or platform passkeys (not TOTP — TOTP can be relayed)

3. Security awareness training: verify requests out-of-band
   - Never approve financial requests via email alone — call on a known number
   - Check unexpected calendar invites and video calls independently

4. Technical controls
   - Disable HTML in email where possible (removes link obfuscation)
   - URL rewriting/sandboxing in email gateway
   - Privileged accounts should have no public OSINT footprint

words.etymology: Spear (from Old English spere, implying precision targeting, contrasted with the wide-net 'phishing'); phishing (a deliberate misspelling of 'fishing', using 'ph' from the phone-phreaking hacker subculture of the 1970s-80s); spear phishing was distinguished from bulk phishing by security researchers in the early 2000s.

words.shortDefinition: Attacker supplies a known session ID pre-login; if the server doesn't rotate it on auth, the attacker hijacks the session.
words.simpleDefinition: In a session fixation attack, the attacker tricks the victim into starting a session with a session ID the attacker already knows — for example, via a URL parameter or a crafted cookie. If the server uses the same session ID after the user logs in without generating a new one, the attacker's pre-known ID becomes a valid authenticated session. The fix is always generating a new, random session ID immediately upon successful authentication.
words.longDefinition: Session fixation was documented by Mitja Kolsek in 2002. The attack flow: (1) attacker obtains a valid unauthenticated session ID from the target server (either by visiting it or by knowing the server accepts externally supplied IDs); (2) attacker sends victim a link containing the session ID (e.g., https://example.com/login?sessionid=ATTACKER_KNOWN_ID); (3) victim clicks the link, logs in, and the server associates the attacker-chosen session ID with the authenticated session; (4) attacker uses the known session ID to access the authenticated session. The root cause is session ID reuse across the authentication boundary. The fix is unconditional: call session_regenerate_id() (or equivalent) immediately after successful authentication, before any privileged actions. Also: do not accept session IDs from URL parameters; session IDs must only travel in cookies with HttpOnly and Secure flags. The OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet mandates session ID rotation on login, privilege level change, and logout. This is distinct from session hijacking (stealing an existing session ID) — fixation uses a pre-planted ID rather than stealing one post-authentication.
words.connector: Think of session fixation like a locksmith handing you a key they already copied before you even move in — once the lock is installed (login), they can enter because they already had the key.
words.techContext: Our session middleware automatically calls regenerateId() on every successful login, making session fixation attacks impossible regardless of how the pre-auth session was established.
words.exampleSentence: The penetration test demonstrated a session fixation vulnerability: the app accepted a sessionId URL parameter and failed to rotate it on login, allowing the tester to hijack authenticated sessions.

codeExample.code:
# Flask: regenerate session on login to prevent session fixation
from flask import session, request, redirect
from flask_login import login_user

@app.route('/login', methods=['POST'])
def login():
    user = authenticate(request.form['username'], request.form['password'])
    if not user:
        return render_template('login.html', error='Invalid credentials'), 401

    # Critical: clear the old session and generate a new session ID
    # before storing any authenticated state
    session.clear()          # removes all session data
    login_user(user)         # sets new authenticated session
    # Flask's session uses a signed cookie; clearing creates a new value
    return redirect('/dashboard')

words.etymology: Session fixation names the attack technique: the attacker 'fixes' (pins) the session identifier to a value they know in advance, before authentication occurs.

words.shortDefinition: Vulnerability where a DNS record points to a deprovisioned cloud resource, allowing an attacker to claim that resource and serve content on the legitimate subdomain.
words.simpleDefinition: A subdomain takeover happens when your DNS still points blog.example.com at a cloud service (like GitHub Pages or an S3 bucket) that you deprovisioned. An attacker claims the vacant resource and can now serve arbitrary content on your subdomain — including phishing pages that inherit your cookies' domain scope.
words.longDefinition: Subdomain takeover is a class of vulnerability that arises from DNS record hygiene failures in environments that use cloud services, CDNs, or SaaS platforms for hosting. When an organization provisions a subdomain (e.g., blog.example.com) with a CNAME pointing to a cloud service (e.g., exampleco.github.io), and then decommissions the cloud resource without removing the DNS record, the CNAME becomes a dangling pointer. An attacker who discovers the dangling record can claim the underlying cloud resource (register exampleco.github.io, claim the S3 bucket, etc.) and now controls what content is served at blog.example.com. The consequences extend well beyond serving defaced pages: the subdomain shares the eTLD+1 (example.com) with the main application. This means: cookies with Domain=.example.com are sent to the attacker's page; the attacker can set cookies for .example.com from the subdomain; if SameSite cookies are not Strict, cross-site requests from the attacker's subdomain are treated as same-site; the SOP (same-origin policy) permits same-origin resource sharing between subdomains of the same domain only when document.domain is manipulated, but the Trust confusion enables social engineering. High-risk cloud services prone to this: GitHub Pages, AWS S3, Heroku, Azure, Cloudfront, Fastly, Shopify, Zendesk. Defense: automate DNS audit — maintain a registry of active DNS records and their corresponding cloud resources; when deprovisioning a cloud resource, remove the DNS record first; scan regularly with tools that check for dangling CNAME targets. Bug bounty programs routinely reward subdomain takeover findings.
words.connector: Think of subdomain takeover like vacating a storefront but leaving the sign up — the next tenant can put whatever merchandise they want in the window, and customers walking by still think they're at the original store.
words.techContext: Our DNS audit script runs weekly and compares active CNAME targets against known-provisioned cloud resources; it alerted us to a dangling GitHub Pages CNAME two days before a bug bounty reporter would have filed the finding.
words.exampleSentence: The subdomain takeover on staging.example.com persisted for six weeks after the staging environment was decommissioned; a researcher claimed the GitHub Pages account and served a demonstration phishing page that appeared at the legitimate staging URL.
words.etymology: Subdomain (a domain name segment below the registered domain, e.g., blog in blog.example.com) + takeover (to seize control of something previously owned by another); the vulnerability was described in web security research in the mid-2010s and became a mainstream bug-bounty finding category.

words.shortDefinition: HTTP response header that prevents a page from being embedded in an iframe, defending against clickjacking.
words.simpleDefinition: X-Frame-Options tells the browser whether the page may be embedded inside an iframe or frame on another site. DENY forbids framing entirely. SAMEORIGIN allows framing only by the same origin. This prevents clickjacking attacks, where an attacker overlays an invisible iframe of the victim site over a convincing decoy to trick users into clicking on hidden buttons.
words.longDefinition: X-Frame-Options was introduced by Microsoft in Internet Explorer 8 (2009) and subsequently standardized in RFC 7034 (2013). It predates the frame-ancestors CSP directive, which is now preferred. Values: DENY (no framing, by any origin), SAMEORIGIN (framing only by same origin), ALLOW-FROM uri (deprecated, inconsistently supported — use CSP frame-ancestors instead). Clickjacking attack: attacker embeds the target site in a transparent iframe positioned over a button on their decoy page; victim clicks what appears to be a 'play' button but is actually the 'transfer funds' button on the target site's interface. Because the victim is already authenticated, the click executes. Notable clickjacking cases: Adobe Flash Player settings panel (2008) enabled microphone/camera activation via clickjacking; the 'likejacking' attacks (2010) tricked users into liking malicious Facebook pages. The modern approach is CSP frame-ancestors because X-Frame-Options cannot restrict to specific third-party domains (ALLOW-FROM is not supported consistently). Recommended policy: add both X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN and CSP frame-ancestors 'self' for defense in depth across older and newer browsers.
words.connector: Think of X-Frame-Options like a 'no photography' sign in a gallery — it tells other browsers not to take a picture of your page and embed it inside their own exhibit.
words.techContext: We set X-Frame-Options: DENY on all pages that perform user actions, and added frame-ancestors 'none' in CSP as a modern equivalent for browsers that ignore the legacy header.
words.exampleSentence: The security scanner reported missing X-Frame-Options headers on the account deletion page, which could allow a clickjacking attack tricking users into deleting their accounts.
words.etymology: X-Frame-Options uses the 'X-' prefix convention for non-standard experimental headers (deprecated by RFC 6648 but retained because it was already widely deployed before standardization).

words.shortDefinition: JavaScript vulnerability where attacker-controlled input modifies Object.prototype, causing unexpected behavior in all objects created thereafter.
words.simpleDefinition: In JavaScript, all objects share a prototype chain. If an attacker can set __proto__.isAdmin = true via a merge, cloneDeep, or JSON parsing operation, every subsequent object in the application may appear to have isAdmin set — potentially bypassing authorization checks or enabling remote code execution in Node.js.
words.longDefinition: Prototype pollution is a JavaScript-specific vulnerability that exploits the mutable prototype chain. Every JavaScript object inherits properties from Object.prototype. If an attacker can influence a property assignment such that the path contains __proto__, constructor.prototype, or Object.prototype, they can inject properties into the base prototype, affecting all subsequently created objects. Vulnerable patterns: deep merge functions that recursively copy properties from user input without filtering special keys; JSON parsing with eval or libraries that honor __proto__; object clone operations on untrusted data. Example: if a vulnerable lodash _.merge is called with { '__proto__': { 'isAdmin': true } }, all subsequent {} literals will have .isAdmin === true. Attack scenarios: (1) Client-side: injected properties can trigger XSS if the application uses them in DOM construction (e.g., innerHTML from a property that defaults to empty string, now polluted to a script tag). (2) Server-side (Node.js): prototype pollution can lead to RCE in template engines (Handlebars, Pug, EJS) that use prototype chain properties for options or code paths; Handlebars RCE via prototype pollution has been demonstrated multiple times with CVEs. (3) Authorization bypass: a check of if (user.isAdmin) trusts a property that defaults to undefined but is now true on the prototype. Mitigations: sanitize user-controlled keys before merge operations (block keys __proto__, constructor, prototype); use Object.create(null) for objects storing untrusted keys (no prototype chain); use Map instead of plain objects for user-keyed data; validate with a schema before deep-merging; update to modern lodash/merge versions that patch the vulnerability.
words.connector: Think of prototype pollution like someone secretly rewriting the employee handbook that all staff share — every worker now thinks certain privileges are allowed because the shared reference was altered, even though their individual employment contracts didn't change.
words.techContext: The security review found that our config merge utility deep-merged untrusted request headers into the defaults object without filtering __proto__, which was patched by adding a blocked-key check before the merge loop.
words.exampleSentence: The prototype pollution vulnerability in the settings endpoint allowed an attacker to set __proto__.debug to true in the shared prototype, enabling verbose error output and stack traces in every subsequent response.
words.etymology: Prototype (from Greek prototypon, 'first impression'; in JavaScript, the object from which other objects inherit properties) + pollution (Latin pollutio, 'defilement'; tainting a shared resource with attacker-controlled data); the term was established in JavaScript security research in the late 2010s.

words.shortDefinition: Challenge presented to distinguish humans from automated bots at login, registration, or high-value action endpoints.
words.simpleDefinition: CAPTCHA (Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart) challenges a user with a task that is easy for humans but difficult for automated bots — distorted text, image selection, or invisible behavioral analysis. Modern CAPTCHAs like Google reCAPTCHA v3 and Cloudflare Turnstile operate in the background, scoring behavior rather than interrupting the user with a visual puzzle.
words.longDefinition: CAPTCHA was coined by Luis von Ahn, Manuel Blum, and colleagues at Carnegie Mellon in 2003. The original visual CAPTCHA (distorted text) has been largely defeated by modern OCR and machine-learning solvers, and CAPTCHA-solving farms offer human solving at pennies per challenge. The field has evolved: (1) reCAPTCHA v2 (image selection challenges); (2) reCAPTCHA v3 (invisible, scores every request 0.0–1.0 based on mouse movement, browsing history, timing; no user interaction required unless score is low); (3) hCaptcha (privacy-focused, GDPR-friendly alternative); (4) Cloudflare Turnstile (passive, cryptographic proof-of-work based). CAPTCHAs are complementary to rate limiting, not a replacement: rate limiting stops volume attacks regardless of automation; CAPTCHA distinguishes human from bot for lower-volume sophisticated attacks. When to require CAPTCHA: account registration (prevent mass fake account creation), login after N failed attempts (slow credential stuffing), password reset, and any endpoint with significant resource cost. CAPTCHA accessibility: audio challenges are required for WCAG 2.1 compliance; invisible behavioral CAPTCHAs have better accessibility but can falsely flag screen reader users. Privacy consideration: reCAPTCHA sends behavioral data to Google; hCaptcha and Turnstile are alternatives for privacy-sensitive applications.
words.connector: Think of CAPTCHA like a bouncer who can spot a robot because humans have nervous little fidgets — micro-hesitations, random mouse movements — that bots execute too perfectly.
words.techContext: We trigger reCAPTCHA v3 on the login endpoint after two failed attempts per account; a score below 0.5 requires the user to solve a v2 challenge before proceeding.
words.exampleSentence: After adding CAPTCHA to the registration flow, the creation of fake accounts for spam dropped by 95%, though we had to tune the threshold to avoid blocking legitimate users on mobile.

codeExample.code:
import httpx

RECAPTCHA_SECRET = 'your_secret_key'
RECAPTCHA_VERIFY_URL = 'https://www.google.com/recaptcha/api/siteverify'

async def verify_recaptcha(token: str, action: str) -> bool:
    """Verify reCAPTCHA v3 token and check action + score."""
    async with httpx.AsyncClient() as client:
        resp = await client.post(RECAPTCHA_VERIFY_URL, data={
            'secret': RECAPTCHA_SECRET,
            'response': token,
        })
    data = resp.json()
    return (
        data.get('success') is True
        and data.get('action') == action
        and data.get('score', 0) >= 0.5   # tune threshold for your traffic
    )

words.etymology: CAPTCHA is a backronym coined at Carnegie Mellon in 2003: Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart, playing on Alan Turing's imitation game.

words.shortDefinition: Browser mechanism that verifies the cryptographic hash of cross-origin scripts or stylesheets before execution.
words.simpleDefinition: Subresource Integrity (SRI) lets you pin a script or stylesheet to a specific cryptographic hash. When the browser loads a cross-origin resource — a CDN-hosted library — it computes the hash of the downloaded file and compares it to the integrity attribute. If they do not match, the resource is blocked. This protects against CDN compromise, where an attacker injects malicious code into a popular library.
words.longDefinition: Subresource Integrity (SRI) is a W3C specification implemented in all modern browsers since 2016. It is applied by adding an integrity attribute to <script> and <link> elements: <script src="https://cdn.example.com/lib.js" integrity="sha384-abc..." crossorigin="anonymous">. The hash is computed over the exact bytes of the resource (after any transfer encoding is removed). Multiple hash algorithms can be specified space-separated; the browser uses the strongest it supports. Supported algorithms: sha256, sha384 (recommended), sha512. The crossorigin="anonymous" attribute is required when using SRI with CORS — without it, for responses requiring CORS headers, the browser cannot read the response body to hash it. When to use SRI: any <script> or <link> loaded from a CDN or external origin. When not to use SRI: resources loaded dynamically at runtime via fetch/XHR (no integrity verification mechanism in the Fetch API for older browsers); resources that change frequently and would require constant hash updates. SRI does not protect against: (1) a compromised package registry (the source your CI/CD builds from); (2) first-party CDN-hosted resources; (3) script loaded from your own origin. For own-origin resources, a nonce-based CSP is the appropriate control. SRI is specifically the defense for the supply-chain risk of third-party CDN compromise.
words.connector: Think of SRI like a signed delivery receipt — you order a specific book, and when it arrives you check the seal number matches what the publisher printed. If someone swapped the contents in transit, the seal won't match.
words.techContext: After the Polyfill.io CDN compromise in 2024, we audited all CDN-hosted scripts and added SRI hashes to every external dependency, blocking any tampered version from executing.
words.exampleSentence: The security policy required SRI attributes on all CDN-hosted scripts; when the CDN was briefly compromised during a supply chain attack, the injected malicious code was blocked by browsers enforcing the hash check.

codeExample.code:
<!-- SRI for a CDN-hosted JavaScript library -->
<!-- Generate hash: openssl dgst -sha384 -binary lib.js | openssl base64 -A -->
<script
  src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/lodash@4.17.21/lodash.min.js"
  integrity="sha384-T1L3DMnEUL72lcNkHzk1fmNk0Hh1HFzU1O7bBbS1BXUK5ABuJ8lmRsApV+TLQAM"
  crossorigin="anonymous"
  referrerpolicy="no-referrer">
</script>

<!-- SRI for a CDN-hosted stylesheet -->
<link
  rel="stylesheet"
  href="https://cdn.example.com/styles.css"
  integrity="sha384-xyz..."
  crossorigin="anonymous">

words.etymology: Subresource Integrity combines 'subresource' (any resource loaded by the page, as opposed to the page itself) with 'integrity' (ensuring the content has not been altered); standardized by the W3C in 2016.

words.shortDefinition: Attack that manipulates a CDN or shared cache into storing a malicious response, delivering it to subsequent legitimate users who request the same resource.
words.simpleDefinition: A web cache serves the same cached response to all users requesting the same resource. If an attacker can craft a request that causes the cache to store a malicious version of a page — by exploiting headers or parameters the cache ignores in its key but the server uses in its response — every subsequent visitor receives the poisoned response.
words.longDefinition: Web cache poisoning (described in depth by James Kettle in research published at PortSwigger, 2018) exploits a mismatch between what a cache uses as its cache key and what the backend server includes in the response. Caches key responses on a subset of the request (typically: method + URL + possibly Accept-Language or Accept-Encoding). If the backend server also uses an unkeyed input — such as X-Forwarded-Host, X-Forwarded-Scheme, X-Original-URL, the Origin header, a query parameter ignored by the cache — in constructing the response body or redirect target, an attacker can manipulate that unkeyed input to produce a malicious response that the cache then serves to all subsequent requests sharing the same cache key. Attack patterns: XSS via poisoned cache (attacker causes the cache to store a response with a malicious JavaScript import from their server; all subsequent visitors execute the script); open redirect via cache (attacker causes a cached redirect to point to a phishing site); CSRF token fixation via cache. The key insight: web cache deception delivers the victim's private data to the attacker; web cache poisoning delivers attacker-controlled content to the victim. Prevention: never include unkeyed inputs in response content; configure caches to vary on all inputs the application uses for responses; use the Vary header to inform caches which request headers affect the response; audit backend response generation for use of arbitrary request headers.
words.connector: Think of web cache poisoning like poisoning a restaurant's supply chain — instead of contaminating one patron's meal, you contaminate the ingredient in the kitchen, so every meal made from that ingredient is dangerous.
words.techContext: Our cache-poisoning audit found that the app echoed the X-Forwarded-Host header into JavaScript import URLs; we removed that behavior and configured Fastly to strip X-Forwarded-Host before forwarding to the origin.
words.exampleSentence: The web cache poisoning exploit required only one crafted request to the CDN edge node: the attacker's X-Forwarded-Host value was reflected into a script src attribute in the response, which the CDN cached and served to the next 10,000 visitors.

codeExample.code:
# Nginx + CDN cache poisoning defense
# Strip unkeyed headers before they reach the application

proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Host   "";   # never pass to backend
proxy_set_header X-Original-URL     "";   # commonly reflected in responses
proxy_set_header X-Rewrite-URL      "";   # IIS variant

# Application must NOT echo any user-controlled header into responses
# Bad (vulnerable):
# response_body = f'<script src="https://{request.headers["X-Forwarded-Host"]}/app.js">'  NEVER DO THIS

# If the app legitimately needs the host, use only the validated Host header
# or a configured BASE_URL environment variable

words.etymology: Web cache poisoning combines 'cache poisoning' (inserting malicious data into a cache so future reads retrieve bad data — a term from DNS cache poisoning, 1990s) with 'web cache' (HTTP caching layer — CDN, reverse proxy, or browser cache); the attack class was systematically catalogued in web security research in the late 2010s.

words.shortDefinition: Time-based One-Time Password; six-digit code generated by an authenticator app, valid for ~30 seconds.
words.simpleDefinition: TOTP generates a six-digit OTP by combining a shared secret (enrolled during setup) with the current Unix timestamp divided into 30-second windows, then applying HMAC-SHA1. Both the authenticator app and the server compute the same value from the same inputs. The code changes every 30 seconds, so a stolen code is useless after the window expires — unless an attacker relays it in real time.
words.longDefinition: TOTP is defined in RFC 6238 (2011), building on HMAC-based OTP (HOTP, RFC 4226). The algorithm: T = floor((current_time - T0) / step_size) where T0 is Unix epoch and step_size is 30 seconds; OTP = HOTP(secret, T) = HMAC-SHA1(secret, T) truncated to 6 digits. Implementation notes: the server should accept a window of ±1 step (±30 seconds) to account for clock drift; storing the previously used OTP and rejecting re-use prevents replay within the same window. TOTP is the dominant TOTP standard — Google Authenticator, Authy, Microsoft Authenticator, 1Password, and Bitwarden all implement RFC 6238. Enrollment: the shared secret is encoded as a base32 string and delivered to the authenticator app via a QR code URI (otpauth://totp/...). Security considerations: (1) the shared secret is a long-term credential — if leaked, all future codes can be generated; store it as securely as a password in the database; (2) TOTP is not phishing-resistant — a real-time proxy can relay codes within the 30-second window; this is how the Uber 2022 breach bypassed TOTP MFA; (3) for phishing-resistant MFA, use WebAuthn/passkeys instead; (4) recovery codes must be generated and stored securely — they bypass TOTP entirely.
words.connector: Think of TOTP like a combination lock that changes its combination every 30 seconds based on a clock synchronized between you and the bank — only someone who has the same clock and secret key can predict the right combination.
words.techContext: We implemented TOTP using a standard RFC 6238 library with a ±1 window for clock drift tolerance and store the last-used OTP to prevent replay attacks within the same time step.
words.exampleSentence: After the phishing simulation showed that 30% of employees entered their TOTP codes on the fake site, the security team began evaluating passkeys as a phishing-resistant replacement.

import pyotp
import time

# Server-side TOTP verification
def verify_totp(
    user_secret: str,
    submitted_code: str,
    last_used_code: str | None
) -> bool:
    totp = pyotp.TOTP(user_secret)

    # valid_window=1 accepts T-1, T, and T+1 (±30 seconds clock drift)
    if not totp.verify(submitted_code, valid_window=1):
        return False

    # Replay prevention: reject the same code within its validity window
    if submitted_code == last_used_code:
        return False

    # Store submitted_code as last_used_code in the database
    return True

words.etymology: TOTP stands for Time-based One-Time Password; it extends HOTP (HMAC-based OTP, RFC 4226) by replacing the counter with the current timestamp, producing time-synchronized codes.

words.shortDefinition: Browser-injected HTTP request headers (Sec-Fetch-Site, Sec-Fetch-Mode, Sec-Fetch-Dest, Sec-Fetch-User) that describe the origin and intent of a request, enabling server-side cross-site request filtering.
words.simpleDefinition: When a browser makes any request, it automatically adds Sec-Fetch-* headers describing where the request came from (same-origin, cross-site, or user navigation) and what kind of resource was requested. A server that checks these headers can reject cross-site requests to endpoints that should never be called cross-site — blocking a class of CSRF, SSRF, and cross-site script inclusion attacks purely by examining request metadata.
words.longDefinition: Sec-Fetch headers (part of the Fetch Metadata Request Headers specification, W3C) are a set of four HTTP request headers that modern browsers attach automatically to every fetch, XHR, navigation, and subresource load. They cannot be set by JavaScript (the 'Sec-' prefix makes them forbidden request headers). Sec-Fetch-Site describes the relationship between the request's origin and the target URL: 'same-origin' (same scheme, host, port), 'same-site' (same registrable domain, different subdomain or scheme), 'cross-site' (different eTLD+1), 'none' (user-initiated navigation with no referrer, e.g., typing a URL directly or following a bookmark). Sec-Fetch-Mode describes how the request was initiated: 'navigate' (browser navigation), 'cors' (CORS-fetched), 'no-cors' (cross-origin non-CORS fetch), 'same-origin', 'websocket'. Sec-Fetch-Dest describes the expected response type: 'document', 'image', 'script', 'style', 'fetch', 'empty' (XHR/fetch with no expected destination), 'worker', etc. Sec-Fetch-User is present (value: '?1') only when the request was triggered by user activation (a click, form submission, or keyboard shortcut), distinguishing active user intent from passive page loads and JavaScript-initiated requests. Server-side resource isolation policies use these headers to allow only expected combinations: an API endpoint that should only be called by same-origin JavaScript can reject any request where Sec-Fetch-Site is 'cross-site'; a navigation endpoint can reject requests where Sec-Fetch-Mode is not 'navigate'. This blocks CSRF (cross-site form submission), XSSI (cross-site script inclusion), and some SSRF scenarios from browser-initiated requests. The defense is complementary to — not a replacement for — SameSite cookies and CSRF tokens.
words.connector: Think of Sec-Fetch headers like a postal service tracking slip automatically attached to every parcel by the post office — the recipient can see where it originated and what service was used, and refuse to open parcels that arrived via an unexpected route.
words.techContext: Our API gateway's resource isolation policy now rejects any request with Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site on endpoints not on the public allowlist, reducing our CSRF attack surface without requiring changes to application-level CSRF token handling.
words.exampleSentence: The Sec-Fetch-Site: cross-site header revealed that a CSRF attempt against the password-change endpoint was arriving from a third-party page; the resource isolation middleware returned 403 before the request reached application code.
